Process case study · October 2026

A portfolio about the work.
And the work behind it.

Turning a body of design work into an interactive portfolio through collaborative, AI-assisted prototyping, iteration, and publishing.

Portfolio storytellingAI-assisted developmentPrototypingDeployment

The challenge

Make the work easy to explore—and easy to maintain.

The project brought visual storytelling, case-study navigation, supporting tools, and practical hosting into one working website. Codex supported implementation and troubleshooting, while the collaboration shaped priorities, feedback, and presentation.

From design intent to working prototype

Shape the experience

Refined the portfolio’s hero, visual presentation, and interaction details to give visitors a clear entry point into the selected work.

Organize the wider story

Created a searchable Treasure Trove project index and a supporting Bounty Board. This process page sits in the unlisted index, preserving the homepage’s focus.

Publish and preserve

Published the updated portfolio to GitHub Pages, archived the previous Dilligaffe homepage, and deployed the new static files to the existing hosting account.

Make handoff practical

Packaged the website and assets in an organized ZIP, shared it with Sindy, and included a Windows launcher for local preview. The launcher still requires verification on Windows.

AI as a collaborator, with human judgment

The workflow used conversational feedback to move between design decisions, implementation, preview, and deployment. The valuable skill was directing the work: clarifying intent, reviewing results, catching assumptions, and deciding what belonged in the final experience.

Collaboratively developed and published an interactive portfolio prototype using AI-assisted design and development, combining storytelling, iteration, version control, and deployment troubleshooting.

Suggested case-study wording. Individual résumé claims should reflect the specific work the person directed or contributed.

Tools and model provenance

Codex by OpenAI

OpenAI Codex supported implementation, browser inspection, file packaging, and deployment work. Session records for both the primary project chat and the hosting chat identify GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra) as the backend model.

OpenAI’s logo is used for tool attribution; this project is not sponsored or endorsed by OpenAI. Brand reference.
This identifies the model recorded in those two chats, not every model involved in the project. The separate voice frontend and image-generation model versions were not verified, so they are not attributed here.

Measuring the process

~3h 40m

Elapsed collaboration at an earlier session checkpoint, including discussion, design, implementation, and troubleshooting. Later handoff work extended beyond this checkpoint.

~1.70M

Uncached input plus output tokens across two recorded chats at a usage checkpoint. Approximately 132.92M additional tokens were recorded as cached input.

Approximate session-log figures, not a complete project total or billing estimate. Cached context is repeated input, not an equivalent volume of newly created work. Voice usage and other chats are not fully accounted for.

What we learned about efficiency

Establish the deployment target and source version early. Use focused inspections, record decisions once, and verify each milestone before moving on. Repeated browser captures and context replay increased the recorded usage; measuring them exposed opportunities to simplify the workflow.

Project-wide retrospective · October 20

Where the tokens went—and what we would change

The earlier two-chat checkpoint above captures one stage of the build. A broader audit through approximately 8:48 p.m. Eastern covered six main chats and ten delegated agents associated with the SindyAI workspace, including research, Figma, portfolio implementation, and hosting.

283.26M

Cumulative input and output tokens across the main chats and delegated agents. This includes cached context reused across many calls.

62%

Of that usage came from the primary portfolio workflow and its six delegated tasks—the largest area to examine for efficiency.

Context reuse dominates the total

Forty automatic review sessions contributed an estimated additional 41.44M tokens after subtracting inherited starting counters. Including those reviews gives a provisional 324.70M-token total: approximately 317.19M cached input, 7.10M uncached input, and 414,390 output tokens. About 97.8% of input was cached.

These are local session counters, not a billing estimate or subscription-allowance calculation. Cached input represents context processed again, not new writing. Reasoning tokens are included in output, not added separately. Review attribution is provisional; separate voice and image-generation service usage may be absent. This is a fixed snapshot, not a live usage dashboard.

What drove the overhead

  • Long-running coordination: the primary chat recorded 799 usage events and 636 tool invocations before this audit. Retaining a large history across many calls increased cumulative input.
  • Delegation: ten workers accounted for 74.30M tokens and 590 tool invocations across the project. They contributed useful work but also required separate context and coordination.
  • Browser interaction: 797 browser-tool invocations occurred across main chats and workers. Repeated page descriptions, setup documentation, and checks added context; an exact browser-only token total was not isolated.
  • Automatic reviews: estimated at 12.8% of the broader cumulative total and about 34% of uncached input. These are required checks, not a category to bypass.
  • Rework from ambiguous context: the scribble reference was initially treated as a standalone image-editing request before being applied as website linework. Confirming the intended artifact from existing project context would have avoided that detour.

A simpler collaboration model

One place for decisions

Keep the primary chat as the project manager and the human collaborator’s point of contact. It owns priorities, accepted decisions, integration, and the final preview.

Small, independent assignments

Use two or three workers when parallel work helps. Each receives one deliverable, relevant files and references, a completion check, and only the context needed. Avoid overlapping ownership of the same files.

Short reports, durable evidence

Workers return the result, changed files, validation, and blockers. Detailed research stays in shared files, with a concise project record preventing repeated discovery.

Milestones before more activity

Research the needed evidence, settle the direction, implement, then review. Use targeted tool results and verify the finished change rather than repeatedly recapturing the whole page.

Lesson learned: optimize for completed, verified outcomes rather than the number of active agents. The audit identifies where usage accumulated; it does not prove that every expensive task was wasteful, and the proposed savings have not yet been measured.

Outcome and remaining checks

The portfolio is published on GitHub Pages and the updated files are served by Dilligaffe over HTTP. The existing ChatGPT Sites preview remains a separate, access-restricted version.

Dilligaffe’s HTTPS certificate still needs verification after enabling the host’s free certificate option. The Windows launcher has not been tested on Windows. Supporting tools use browser-local storage and do not yet sync between devices.
